title: Chore Chart for a Family of 6 (Free Editable Printable)
meta_description: A free, editable chore chart for a family of 6, 7, or 8. Give everyone a job that fits their age, rotate the tough ones fairly, and track it all on one page.
h1: Chore Chart for a Family of 6
intro: Our house runs as a family of six — two parents and four kids, from a nine-year-old up to an eighteen-year-old — and for stretches, when we had foster children living with us, we were a family of seven or eight. So a chore chart for a family of 6 isn't a hypothetical for us; it's the tool that keeps a loud, busy, mixed-age household from quietly turning into a place where the same two people do everything and resent it. The chart below is a blank, editable grid: you name the jobs, you name the people, and you decide who does what. What we can add is the part no template prints — how we actually split work across six-plus people of very different ages, how we keep the older kids from getting stuck with every hard job, and why, in our experience, this works best as a way for the parents to track the family rather than a sticker board built to bribe the kids into caring.

sections.heading: Give each person their own row — and match the job to the kid, not just the age
sections.body:
In a big family, the classic mistake is one generic chore list for the whole family of 6 stuck to the fridge — dishes, trash, vacuum — that technically belongs to everyone and therefore to no one. The version that works for us gives every single person their own line, with their name on top and their own jobs underneath. That's why this chart is built with a column per person and scales past six without getting crowded.

The jobs on each line should fit the kid, not just fill the grid. Our youngest started with looking after himself and his own space; the older ones carry real, load-bearing work — cooking, dishes, yard, helping with repairs. We don't treat any of it as a way to get the house clean. We treat it as reps for adulthood — the actual goal is a capable adult, not an unloaded dishwasher. That reframe changes what you'll tolerate along the way: you expect the early work to be redone, and you let competence build over years. Our nine-year-old now gathers every trash can in the house and takes it out with zero reminders — and that only happened because he practiced the small version for a very long time.

sections.heading: Rotate the jobs no one wants (so your most capable kid isn't punished for being capable)
sections.body:
The specific trap in a large family is that your most reliable kid quietly becomes your unpaid manager. The older ones can actually do the hard jobs well, so the hard jobs drift toward them — and they notice. That's what the rotation option is for: drop the genuinely unpopular jobs (scrubbing the bathroom, hauling trash, the after-dinner kitchen) into a pool that shifts down the family each week, so no one owns the worst job forever.

Keep a couple of things fixed, though. Little kids still have anchor tasks that match where they are — a five-year-old isn't rotating into mowing — while the rotating pool moves only among the kids who can handle those jobs. And once a kid hits the teen years, we've found the family chart mostly stops working anyway; at that point we switch them to something closer to a job, with a monthly payment and tasks we ask for in advance, rather than a row on the same grid as their younger siblings. In one household you can easily have a nine-year-old on real-time prompts, an eleven-year-old who genuinely loves designing and running her own chart, and a teen on the job model — all at the same time. Meet each kid where they actually are.

sections.heading: The chart is your dashboard — motivation comes from being part of the household
sections.body:
Here's the stance that runs through everything we build: the chart is mostly for you, the parent. With six-plus people in the house, you cannot hold everyone's progress in your head. The chart's real job is to let you glance at the week and see who's keeping up and who needs a nudge — it's a dashboard, not a bribe.

We deliberately keep motivation off the chart. What drives the work is the plain expectation that this is our home and the load is shared — the jobs belong to the whole family, not to whoever earns a sticker. We keep rewards and screen time in a completely separate lane; kids don't work for screens. Allowance exists, but it's tied to the overall pattern — how well someone follows through, whether they stay on top of things, the attitude they bring — rather than priced out task by task. And one small, free lever prevents an enormous number of fights in a busy house: advance notice. 'In about an hour we're doing the kitchen' lands completely differently than 'go do the kitchen right now,' because it gives everyone time to shift gears.

sections.heading: Build a large family chore chart that survives a normal, chaotic week
sections.body:
A big family generates a lot of real life — a sick kid, a travel weekend, a holiday, a week that simply falls apart. The most common way a chore system dies is that someone builds the perfect version, real life knocks it over once, and everyone decides it 'didn't work.' It worked fine; it just wasn't built to be knocked down and stood back up. So design for the restart: a chart you can walk away from for a week and resume without ceremony beats an elaborate one you're afraid to break.

Two more things we learned the hard way. First, keep it visible — on paper, posted where people actually walk past it. Apps tend to vanish into a parent's phone where the kids never see them, which defeats the point. Second, a posted routine isn't only for the kids; it lets the adults hand off cleanly. When we were fostering and our household grew to seven or eight, a predictable, written pattern was what let either of us step in and run the evening without a negotiation — and, more than we expected, that same structure is what helped anxious kids settle and start to trust that the day would go the way it always did. Aim for steady progress over a flawless chart. In a house this size, a restartable, visible large family chore chart beats a perfect one every time.

faq.q: How do I make a chore chart for a family of 6?
faq.a: Start by giving every person their own space on the chart instead of writing one shared list for the whole family of 6. Down each person's line, fill in jobs that fit their age and ability — self-care and their own space for the youngest, real household jobs for the older kids. Put the genuinely unpopular chores into a weekly rotation so they're shared, and leave a few age-appropriate anchor tasks fixed. Then print it, post it somewhere everyone passes, and use it mainly to track who's keeping up. Our chart is a blank, editable grid, so you fill in your own family's names and jobs rather than following a fixed list.

faq.q: How do you divide chores fairly in a large family?
faq.a: Two moves do most of the work. First, match the jobs to each kid's stage, so no one is set up to fail and no one is left bored. Second, rotate the jobs everyone hates — bathrooms, trash, the after-dinner kitchen — so your most capable kid doesn't silently inherit them just for being good at them. Fairness in a big family isn't identical chores for everyone; it's an age-appropriate load for each person plus a fair share of the miserable stuff. And keep in mind that teens usually work better on a job-style arrangement than on the same chart as the little ones.

faq.q: Does this chart work for a family of 7 or 8?
faq.a: Yes. The chart is built with a line per person and scales past six, so a family of 7 or 8 — or a blended or multigenerational household, or a foster placement that suddenly grows the count — works the same way. Add a column for each additional person, give them age-appropriate jobs, and widen the rotation pool. We've run our own house at six normally and at seven or eight while fostering, and the structure holds as long as each person has their own line and the hardest jobs keep moving.
